judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Icon-only Instagram link in the FOLLOW ECHO sidebar row. The crop shows a grey (#9d9d9c) tile on the white page with a white camera glyph cut out of it; both the tile against the page and the glyph against the tile are 2.71:1, below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks for the visual information identifying a control (G207). The live HTML serves the same inline SVG with the same .st0 fill #9d9d9c, and the screenshot is a fully styled render, so the capture matches what users receive. I looked for a way out: the FOLLOW ECHO text above the row labels the group but does not tell the links apart, so the icon is still the only visual identification of this control. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos on the assumption that brand guidelines dictate their colours, but says a logo is not exempt when the author chose the low-contrast variant; a neutral grey rendition is the site's own styling, not a colour these brands require. No reason holds up, so the claim names a real failure.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale:
Lead teaser image (generic stock photo of a garda seen from behind) inside the link to the hijacking story. Its alt is the article's photo caption, with literal '

' tags: an appeal for witnesses at Curraheen Road Sports Grounds between 1pm and 2pm. I opened the article: the caption belongs to this same story, so it is not text from another item. The claim is true of the capture (the appeal, place and time are not in the picture). I lean to a failure, because the alt is a caption rather than an alternative and screen readers announce the stray markup. But a concrete counter-reason holds up in part: the image is a generic stock photo whose only information is 'gardaí', which the alt does convey, and it sits inside a link whose text gives the story. Competent auditors would split on whether that fails F30's replace-the-image test. The story has since rotated off the live homepage, but the live markup still emits caption alts with escaped

tags the same way, so the capture shows what users received.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Teaser photo inside the link 'Rent inflation in Cork city up 11% year-on-year'. The crop shows a key in a door lock with a small house-shaped keyring, a door edge and a blurred figure behind: that is what the alt 'House key with home keyring in keyhole on wood door, copy space' says. 'Copy space' is stock-photo jargon, not a mismatch. The claim is false, and the alt is an accurate alternative for an image that supplements the headline, so 1.1.1 is met. The model had the crop and judged wrongly. The story has rotated off the live homepage; nothing suggests the capture differed from what users received.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Cork Lives teaser photo (file 'OthelloPic': people in costume by a stone building) inside a link whose visible text is the same headline quote the alt repeats: 'I left LA to be an actor in Cork ... I've always loved the rain!'. Literally, the alt is a quote, and LA and the rain are not in the picture, so the sentence holds. The skeptic's counter-reasons: the alt names the story's subject (the actress quoted, who appears to be in the cast photo); the image only supplements a link that already carries the same words; and duplicating the headline is a redundancy problem (H2 suggests a null alt), not something a 1.1.1 failure names. I lean to a pass, but auditors would reasonably split on whether a headline-as-alt that says nothing about the photo is an equivalent. The live homepage still serves the same image and alt.

judgments.label: uncertain

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Header icon link named 'instagram' (fa icon, aria-label) to https://www.instagram.com/echolive.ie/. The snapshot has three such links in the accessibility tree (header, the FOLLOW ECHO sidebar 'Instagram', and the footer under 'Follow Us') plus a hidden subnav copy. Their only URL difference is that the sidebar adds '?hl=en', which just sets Instagram's interface language on the same @echolive.ie profile: the same or an equivalent resource under R1. The preceding headings also differ (none, FOLLOW ECHO, Follow Us), so they are not even one set. The claim that they lead to two different places is wrong; the link's purpose is clear. The model had the hrefs and misread a language parameter as a different destination. The live HTML has the same links.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Search button of the embedded myhome property-search widget in the sidebar: white bold 13px text on a #009cdb button. The crop of the screenshot shows exactly that, and the computed ratio is 3.10:1. 13px bold is not large text (that needs 14pt bold, about 18.7px), so 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1. I looked for a reason it passes: the colours are solid, not an anti-aliasing artefact, there is no incidental or logotype exception, and the widget is in the page's own DOM (not an iframe), so it is part of the page's content. My fetch of the live raw HTML does not render the script-injected widget, but the capture is a fully styled browser render and nothing suggests a different style for users. The claim names the failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The 'MORE' item of the main navigation (href='#', a hover dropdown toggle). Its own list item, which the rubric counts as programmatically determined context, contains the dropdown's links (Advertise with us, Mini Marathon 2026, Find a House, Find a Job, Competitions ... Echo Sport Podcast), exposed in the accessibility tree. So the link text with its list item tells users it opens more site sections. The claim's 'nothing around it does' is false. Using a link rather than a button for a menu toggle is a 4.1.2 matter, not 2.4.4. The model had that list-item text in its context. The live HTML is the same.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Main-navigation link 'Wow!' (shown as WOW!) to /wow/, a section whose page title is 'WoW - Echolive', in a list of section links (Cork News, Cork Sport, Cork Lives, Nostalgia...). The link text is the destination section's name, which tells users where it goes: to the Wow! section. If someone still finds the name opaque, sighted users have exactly the same information, so the purpose would be ambiguous to users in general, the criterion's exception. The claim is literally true (the text does not explain the section's content), but 2.4.4 does not require that. The checker applied a stricter rule than WCAG's. The live HTML is the same.
